extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, translators, and general readers interested in the history, forms, and features of Chinese literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative dimensions for composing or assessing Chinese literary works (poetry, prose, drama, and fiction) across historical periods, with attention to forms, language register, thematic concerns, and ideological prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical poetic form and meter (shi, couplets, fixed line-lengths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shi poems often composed of couplets with lines of fixed character counts (four, five, seven characters) and a formal structure of end rhymes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Shijing's couplets with lines of four characters; emergence of five-character and seven-character lines; regulated verse and line-length conventions are central formal constraints in classical Chinese poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bi / xing (image-to-emotion technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many early poems establish the later tradition of starting with a description of nature that leads into emotionally expressive statements, known as bi, xing, or sometime bixing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indirect technique — giving an image or scene that opens the poem and then moving into feeling — is a persistent compositional device across Chinese poetic history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density and placement of imagery in jueju (quatrains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quatrains (jueju) conventionally contain about two distinct images or thoughts per line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wang Wei's quatrains are cited as exemplars; the form's compactness requires concentrated imagery and often a caesura or internal division of thought within lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonality and regulated verse (jintishi) constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: New-style regulated verse (jintishi) is tonally regulated and often uses seven-character lines with strict tonal patterns and parallelism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Du Fu excelled at regulated verse and use of the seven-character line; such poems often employ denser allusion and formal parallel structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ci form: matching lyric to musical templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Ci poetry developed from musical songs and uses a variety of standard song-templates with distinctive and variously set meters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song dynasty ci flourished as a few hundred songs became standard templates; successful ci typically fit the melodic/metered pattern and its emotive conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter, caesura, and dramatic rhythm (Chu Ci and six-character lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain lyric traditions (e.g., Chu Ci) employ six-character-per-line meters divided into couplets separated by a strong caesura, producing a driving and dramatic rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter and mid-line pause shape the poem's momentum; the Chu Ci's emotional intensity is tied to its rhythmic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusiveness and intertextual density
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems, especially by poets like Du Fu and Li Shangyin, often use dense allusions and obscure references which contribute to their depth and posthumous fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High allusiveness can increase complexity and require knowledgeable readers; different periods favored more or less allusiveness (e.g., Tang high culture prized refinement and allusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical prose style: simplicity, directness, and force
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Tang onward there was an ideal of replacing ornate prose with simple, direct, and forceful prose based on earlier models from the Hundred Schools and Han historiography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Han Yu exemplified the neoclassical return to concise, organized discourses; clarity, economy, and strong organization are prized in classical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical method and argumentative rigor (philosophical prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical and polemic prose (e.g., Mozi, Mencius, Zhuang Zhou) is expected to show well-reasoned, carefully developed discourse, solid methodological reasoning, and skillful use of comparisons, anecdotes, and allegory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities were models for effective essay-writing across eras; logical structure and persuasive devices are central evaluative features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vernacular language for modern realism and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern literature moved toward the vernacular (baihua) to represent contemporary reality and to make literature more directly relevant and readable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hu Shih and Chen Duxiu promoted vernacular writing as capable of producing 'living literature'; vernacular prose was seen as better suited to social engagement and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism and social engagement (modern/May Fourth and leftist fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much May Fourth and leftist fiction emphasized realism, addressed social problems, and used literature as a vehicle for political critique or reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socialist realism explicitly required art to concentrate on contemporary events realistically, expose ills of nonsocialist society, and promote a communist future; May Fourth writers used realism to confront social problems and national crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic emphasis: moral humanism, optimism, and group behavior (classical fiction audiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical and vernacular readers often appreciated themes of relative optimism, moral humanism, emphasis on group behavior, and welfare of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thematic preferences shaped narrative choices in extended prose narratives and novels from late imperial periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelistic worldbuilding and believable extended narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel as an extended prose narrative is evaluated by its ability to realistically create a believable world of its own and to explore social, moral, and philosophical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chinese novels from the 14th–18th centuries evolved long-form realism and deep social insight (e.g., Dream of the Red Chamber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid/form-blending genres (travel literature, drama, opera)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain genres intentionally blend forms — e.g., travel literature combines diary and narrative prose; modern 'civilized drama' hybridizes Chinese operatic drama with Western-style spoken drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness is judged by how well the hybrid melds its constituent conventions and serves its expressive or social purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation with language and narrative modes (modernist and avant-garde tendencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: 20th-century movements (New Sensationists, misty poets, avant-garde writers) valued experimentation with vernacular, obscurity, subjective realism, and modernist narrative methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such works are often assessed on innovation in language, narrative voice, and psychological depth rather than traditional realist/social standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of female subjectivity and new archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern women writers foregrounded female subjectivity (e.g., 'New Woman', 'Modern Girl'), exploring domestic relations, sexuality, and social roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation includes how directly and complexly female interiority and social position are rendered (examples: Ding Ling, Eileen Chang).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political / ideological function (Yan'an Talks and Maoist guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mao's Yan'an Talks articulated five categories of creative consideration for socialist cultural production: class stand, attitude, audience, work style, and popularization/massification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this rubric, literature is evaluated primarily by political alignment, class perspective, attitude toward socialism, who the work addresses, its style appropriate to mass audiences, and its capacity to popularize Party goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Three prominences' and ideological clarity during Maoist cultural campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'three prominences' principle required texts to demonstrate the struggle between revolutionary and reactionary forces in a stark and dichotomous manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works were to foreground revolutionary heroes and ideological conflict clearly and prominently; this was an applied evaluative standard during model-work campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative formula 'revolution plus love'
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurrent narrative formula combined revolutionary mission with romantic love: the story begins with conflict between revolution and love, calls for devotion to revolution, and ends with the couple working together for the revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula was both a literary trope and a political mandate; evaluation considers fidelity to the formula and its rhetorical and ideological effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of translation and foreign forms as innovation/modernization tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Translation of Western and other foreign genres (e.g., science fiction, realism) and incorporation of foreign forms were used as mechanisms for modernization and new literary strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late Qing and early 20th-century writers' use of translated forms is an evaluative axis: how effectively they adapt foreign modes to local concerns and language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical and performative requirements in operatic/qu form(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres derived from performance (qu, sanqu, opera) require attention to musicality, performative rhythm, and suitability for stage or song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yuan qu and later sanqu are judged by their relation to operatic conventions and by their capacity to function as performed pieces (meter, melody, cadence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calligraphic/visual integration (painter-poets and the three perfections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combined arts (poetry, painting, calligraphy) in painter-poets emphasize the integration of verbal and visual aesthetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of such works considers the harmony between image, inscription, and calligraphic execution as part of literary-artistic merit.
